stages.sub: How weak legal systems choke off savings and why governments turn to foreign investment instead.

steps.q: A farmer in a developing country has no official document proving she owns her land. If a local official seizes it tomorrow, what can she do about it?
steps.right: Very little, she has no legal claim to enforce
steps.wrong: She can easily win it back in court
steps.hint: Without any registered ownership, what proof does she have to point to?

steps.q: A bank normally lends against land or a house as security. If that farmer cannot prove she owns anything, will the bank lend her money to expand her farm?
steps.right: No, it will refuse or charge very high rates
steps.wrong: Yes, it will lend on the same terms as anyone else
steps.hint: Banks want something to seize if a loan is not repaid. What happens when there is nothing to point to as collateral?

steps.q: The Harrod-Domar model says growth needs savings to fund investment. If most people cannot open savings accounts or get loans, what happens to the pool of funds available for domestic investment?
steps.right: It stays too small to fund the investment needed
steps.wrong: It grows quickly through informal saving instead
steps.hint: Investment has to be funded from somewhere. If banking is closed off to most people, where does that funding come from?

steps.q: Domestic savings cannot fund enough investment, and capital flight drains funds abroad. If a government wants factories and infrastructure built anyway, whose money could it attract from outside instead?
steps.right: Foreign firms investing directly in the country
steps.wrong: Foreign governments giving free aid grants
steps.hint: Think of a firm building its own factory abroad rather than a government handing over money.

steps.q: A foreign car company builds a factory in the country, bringing its own funds, machinery and trained managers. Does the country now depend only on its own limited domestic savings to get this factory built?
steps.right: No, the investment came from outside the savings gap
steps.wrong: Yes, domestic savings still had to pay for it
